Next: The record behind this act.

Article 6(c) prohibits inflicting on the group conditions of life calculated to bring about its physical destruction in whole or in part. Track 2 applicants are disproportionately poor, female, and offered minimal housing or income support before approval for death.
The documentary stage below stitches the ACT IV chapter film. Then walk the evidence scene-by-scene. Atmosphere is not the proof; primary sources are.
Poverty share, female skew, material-resources and housing quintiles, palliative access gap.

About one in three Track 2 recipients reviewed reported poverty as a contributing factor (Ontario Chief Coroner, Vulnerability and MAiD, 2024). Housing and income offers were minimal or absent in most files.
Ontario Track 2 skews female, poor, and isolated — clinical isolation on the coroner record, not a composite graphic. Housing crisis and gendered poverty in the same files.

Track 2 over-representation in the lowest material-resources quintile (28.4%) and highest residential-instability quintile (48.3%) — MDRC Marginalization Data Perspectives. Baseline for each quintile is 20% of the population.
Fewer than three in ten who could benefit receive palliative care (CIHI / Health Canada estimates), while federal MAID provision counts have risen year over year since 2016.

Film is memorial tone only. Article 6(c) is argued from MDRC vulnerability and marginalization data , housing and poverty shares , and palliative access set against rising MAID volume. This act does not use composite “attrition vector” charts or AI flag stills.
